prompt: In `secret.yaml`, the client secret is written as `bm90LWEtcmVhbC1zZWNyZXQ=`. What does that encoding protect it from?
hint: The section turned it back into words with one command.

choices.text: A glance over somebody's shoulder, and nothing more
choices.why: Base64 is an encoding with no key: `base64 -d` reverses it on any Linux machine, as the capture did.

choices.text: Anyone without the cluster's encryption key
choices.why: There is no key in base64. Encryption of etcd is a separate setting, and it does nothing about the copies in a repository or a log.

choices.text: Anyone not allowed to `get secrets` in the namespace
choices.why: That is Kubernetes RBAC on the cluster's copy, not the encoding; the file in the repository has no RBAC at all.

choices.text: Being used from outside the tenant
choices.why: Entra ID accepts a valid client secret from anywhere that can reach it; the encoding plays no part.

prompt: According to the help of `az ad sp create-for-rbac` captured in the section, for how many years is a client secret valid when nobody chooses?
hint: Read the `Default:` on the line after `--years`.

prompt: Where does a client secret placed in `secret.yaml` end up? Choose every place the section names.

choices.text: In the repository and every clone of it, if the file was committed
choices.why: Git keeps every committed version, so deleting the file later leaves the secret in history.

choices.text: In every pod that mounts the Secret
choices.why: Mounting it is the purpose of the Secret, so each such pod holds the secret in its environment.

choices.text: In a CI log that printed the environment
choices.why: One of the accidental copies the section lists, and among the hardest to find afterwards.

choices.text: In the managed identity, which keeps it to expire it
choices.why: A managed identity has no client secret at all; the secret belongs to an application registration, which records only its metadata and end date.

choices.text: In the federated credential of the service account
choices.why: A federated credential holds an issuer, a subject and an audience, and no secret of any kind.

prompt: To avoid a secret, a team grants `Storage Blob Data Contributor` on the receipts container to the cluster's kubelet identity. What did they actually grant?
hint: Think about who can reach the Instance Metadata Service from a pod.

choices.text: Write access to the receipts for the order API's pods alone
choices.why: The kubelet identity belongs to the nodes, not to any one workload; nothing in the grant names the order API.

choices.text: Write access to the receipts for every pod on those nodes
choices.why: By default every pod in an AKS cluster can reach the metadata service, and through it the identities the node carries.

choices.text: Nothing, because a kubelet identity cannot hold Azure roles
choices.why: It holds roles routinely: pulling from a registry is a role assignment on exactly this identity.

choices.text: Write access for the kubelet, which no pod can use
choices.why: The kubelet is not the only process that can ask the metadata service; any pod not blocked from it can.

prompt: Tired of outages when secrets expire, a team creates every new client secret with `--end-date 2299-12-31`. What have they traded?
hint: The section names two ways a secret fails. Which one did they remove, and which one did they make worse?

choices.text: Nothing: Entra ID still rotates the secret on its own, once a year, without being asked
choices.why: Entra ID rotates nothing; a client secret is valid until its end date or until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: Planned outages for unplanned ones, since a far date is refused
choices.why: The help offers that very date as an example, and the command accepts it.

choices.text: An outage on a known date for a password that works as long as any copy survives
choices.why: The expiry outage is gone, and every copy listed in the section now stays valid for centuries.

choices.text: A rotation by hand for one done by the workload identity webhook
choices.why: The webhook never touches client secrets; it injects a projected token and four variables.

prompt: On AKS, the service account `orders` carries the `azure.workload.identity/client-id` annotation, and a pod using it has no `azure.workload.identity/use` label. What does the webhook add to that pod?
hint: The documentation calls the label required.

choices.text: The four variables, but no token volume
choices.why: The webhook does not split its work that way; it mutates a labelled pod fully and leaves others alone.

choices.text: Everything, since the annotation is what it reads
choices.why: The annotation supplies the client id, but the webhook only acts on pods carrying the label.

choices.text: Nothing: only labelled pods are mutated
choices.why: Microsoft's documentation says only pods with the label are mutated, whatever their service account says.

choices.text: A token for the API server's audience instead
choices.why: Every pod gets that token from Kubernetes itself, with or without the webhook; it is not what the webhook adds.

prompt: Complete the audience of the projected volume in `orders.yaml`, the one the federated credential will be written for: `audience: api://___`
hint: It describes what the token is for: exchanging it at Entra ID.

prompt: `decode.py` printed `sub: system:serviceaccount:shop:orders` from the token. Why does that prove nothing about which pod wrote the file?
hint: Look at the last line the program printed.

choices.text: Because nobody checked the signature over those claims
choices.why: Anybody can write those claims; only the signature, checked with the issuer's public key, ties them to the cluster.

choices.text: Because `sub` is encrypted and the program showed a guess
choices.why: Nothing in the token is encrypted; the claims are encoded JSON, which is why the program could print them.

choices.text: Because kind writes a fake `sub` that AKS would correct
choices.why: The `sub` came from kind's own API server and is the real service account; AKS would write the same string.

choices.text: Because the token was copied to the laptop, which changes it
choices.why: Copying a token changes nothing in it; the problem is that nobody checked who made it.

prompt: A projected token has `expirationSeconds: 3600`. Following the rule in the Kubernetes documentation, how many minutes after it was issued does the kubelet ask for a new one?
hint: 80% of the lifetime, unless the token is older than 24 hours first.

prompt: The pod holds two tokens with the same `iss`, the same `sub` and the same `kid`. Which claim lets Entra ID refuse the one Kubernetes mounts for the API server?
hint: Compare the two decoded tokens line by line.

choices.text: `exp`, because the API server's token lasts a year
choices.why: That lifetime is kind's extension and AKS turns it off; a token of the right lifetime with the wrong audience is still refused.

choices.text: `kid`, because each audience is signed with its own key
choices.why: The capture showed the same `kid` on both: one cluster key signs them all.

choices.text: `kubernetes.io`, because it names the pod rather than the identity
choices.why: Both tokens carry the same `kubernetes.io` block, and Entra ID does not compare it with anything.

choices.text: `aud`, which names the API server instead of Entra ID
choices.why: The federated credential names an audience, and a token for another one matches no record.

prompt: What does a federated identity credential on the managed identity `shop-orders` hold?

choices.text: A certificate that the cluster presents when it signs in
choices.why: No certificate is involved and the cluster never signs in; Entra ID reads the issuer's published keys instead.

choices.text: An issuer, a subject and a list of audiences
choices.why: Three strings, compared with the token's `iss`, `sub` and `aud`, and no secret of any kind.

choices.text: The cluster's public signing keys, copied at creation
choices.why: Entra ID fetches the keys from the issuer when it needs them, which is why a key rotation needs no change to the credential.

choices.text: A client secret that expires with the projected token
choices.why: There is no secret in it; avoiding one is the point of federation.

prompt: Match each change made to `identity.bicep` with what happened when it was compiled, or would happen afterwards.

pairs.right: warning BCP089, with the right name suggested
compiles; Entra ID finds no matching record
compiles; no published keys for Entra ID to fetch
warning BCP036, a string where a bool belongs

right_distractors: compiles; Entra ID adds the missing s itself
the template is not written at all

prompt: Suppose the lab had a real tenant, and a federated credential named kind's issuer `https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`. Why would Entra ID still refuse the pod's token?
hint: Look at where the discovery document says the keys are.

choices.text: Because kind signs with RS256, which Entra ID does not accept
choices.why: RS256 is the one algorithm Entra ID's documentation says is supported for this exchange.

choices.text: Because the token's audience is wrong for Entra ID
choices.why: The projected volume asked for `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, the audience a credential expects.

choices.text: Because a subject in a kind cluster has a different format
choices.why: The `sub` is `system:serviceaccount:shop:orders`, the same format AKS writes.

choices.text: Because it cannot reach the issuer to fetch the keys
choices.why: The name only resolves inside a cluster and the key set sits at a private Docker address, so the signature can never be checked.

prompt: `shop-orders` already has federated credentials for the `orders` service account in 7 clusters and for a `reports` service account in 5 of them. Within the documented maximum, in how many more clusters can `orders` be trusted?
hint: Each credential is one service account in one cluster, and the documented maximum is per managed identity.

prompt: A template declares three federated credentials on `shop-orders` in a loop, and some deployments fail with HTTP 409 while others succeed. What is the fix?
hint: The documentation describes this failure for one parent identity and not for several.

choices.text: Wait a few minutes between deployments for propagation
choices.why: Propagation delays the first token request; it does not make the creation itself conflict.

choices.text: Give each credential a different audience
choices.why: The audience has no bearing on a 409: the conflict comes from concurrent writes to one identity.

choices.text: Create them in sequence, each depending on the last
choices.why: Concurrent creation under one identity is refused with 409; the documentation's remedy is a sequential order.

choices.text: Put each credential on a different cluster's identity
choices.why: Moving them to other identities avoids the conflict, but the order API would then have three identities instead of one.

prompt: Put the exchange in the order it happens on Azure, from the order API's first call to Blob Storage.
items: The SDK reads AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE and opens the token
The SDK sends the token to Entra ID as client_assertion
Entra ID fetches the issuer's public keys
Entra ID checks the signature, then the federated credential
Entra ID returns an access token with expires_in
The SDK writes the receipt with an Authorization: Bearer header
trap: Comparing the subject before checking the signature: no claim can be believed until the signature over all of them is verified.

prompt: After moving to workload identity, a pod still mounts the old `orders-entra` Secret beside the new token. Which credential does `DefaultAzureCredential` use?
hint: The section gives the start of its list for Python.

choices.text: The token, because workload identity always takes precedence
choices.why: Workload identity is second in the list; the environment credential is tried first.

choices.text: Neither: it refuses to choose when both are present
choices.why: It does not refuse; it uses the first credential in its list that has what it needs.

choices.text: Whichever was mounted last into the pod
choices.why: The order is fixed by the library, not by the order of mounts.

choices.text: The client secret: the environment credential comes first
choices.why: With `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID` and `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` present, the first credential in the list signs in with the secret.

prompt: In the token request, what is sent as `client_assertion`?

choices.text: The projected service account token, as it is in the file
choices.why: The file's contents go as the assertion, which is why the request reads `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`.

choices.text: A JWT the SDK signs with the managed identity's private key
choices.why: A managed identity hands the pod no private key; the assertion is the token Kubernetes signed.

choices.text: The client id of `shop-orders`, encoded as a JWT
choices.why: The client id travels in `client_id`, a separate field.

choices.text: An access token from the Instance Metadata Service
choices.why: Workload identity does not use the metadata service at all; that is the managed identity flow.

prompt: A federated credential was created a minute ago. The first token request fails with `AADSTS70021`, and the same pod succeeds a few minutes later with nothing changed. What happened?
hint: Both the AKS and the Entra ID documentation mention a delay after adding a credential.

choices.text: The subject was wrong and Entra ID corrected it
choices.why: Entra ID never corrects a subject; a wrong one fails every time, not only the first.

choices.text: The credential had not yet propagated, so retries with a short wait are the fix
choices.why: The documentation describes exactly this window and recommends a short wait and retries.

choices.text: The projected token had expired and the kubelet renewed it
choices.why: A fresh pod's token lasts an hour; and an expired token is not what `AADSTS70021` describes.

choices.text: The role assignment had not taken effect yet
choices.why: A missing role is refused by the storage account after a token is issued, not by Entra ID at the exchange.

prompt: Which of these does Entra ID check before it issues the access token? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The token's signature, with a key from the issuer's key set
choices.why: The first check: without it, none of the claims can be believed.

choices.text: That `iss`, `sub` and `aud` match a federated credential on the identity
choices.why: Compared case-sensitively and in full with the three strings of a credential.

choices.text: That the token is not past its `exp`
choices.why: An expired token is refused, which is why the kubelet keeps the file fresh.

choices.text: That the pod's address is inside the cluster's virtual network
choices.why: The exchange is decided by the token, not by where the request came from.

choices.text: That the token's `kubernetes.io` pod uid still exists
choices.why: Entra ID cannot see the cluster's objects; that check is one only the cluster's API server makes.

prompt: Match each variable the webhook adds with what it tells the SDK.

pairs.right: the address of the sign-in endpoint

right_distractors: the storage account to write to

prompt: The annotation on `orders` was changed to a new identity's client id an hour ago, and the running pods still act as the old one. What do they need?

choices.text: A restart, since the webhook only acts when a pod is created
choices.why: The documentation says a changed annotation takes effect only after the pod is restarted.

choices.text: A new federated credential on the old identity
choices.why: The old identity is the one they should stop using; nothing on it needs changing.

choices.text: A key rotation with `az aks oidc-issuer rotate-signing-keys`
choices.why: Rotation changes the cluster's signing keys, not which identity a pod's variables name.

choices.text: Nothing more than waiting for the kubelet to refresh the token
choices.why: A refreshed token carries the same audience and subject, and the variables in the pod do not change.

prompt: To save work, a team writes one federated credential with the subject `system:serviceaccount:shop:*`, meaning every service account in `shop`. What does it match?
hint: Read what the command line's help says about how the subject is compared.

choices.text: Every service account in the namespace `shop`
choices.why: The subject is compared exactly, so the asterisk is a character, not a pattern.

choices.text: No token at all, since no service account is called `*`
choices.why: Exact matching makes it a literal subject; the preview claims matching expression is the separate way to write a pattern.

choices.text: Only the first service account created in `shop`
choices.why: There is no notion of order in the comparison; the string has to equal the token's `sub`.

choices.text: Every service account, but only for the default audience
choices.why: The audience is compared separately and does not change how the subject is read.

prompt: Of the three answers compared at the end of the lesson, which one leaves nothing stored and lets only one service account in one cluster use it?

choices.text: A client secret in a Kubernetes Secret
choices.why: The secret is stored in every copy and works for anybody holding one.

choices.text: The kubelet identity
choices.why: Nothing is stored, but every pod on the node can use it.

choices.text: Workload identity
choices.why: The token is made for one service account, and the credential trusts only that one in one cluster.

choices.text: Pod-managed identity
choices.why: Deprecated since 2022, and not one of the table's three; it also ran through the node's metadata service.
